issues.legal_issue: A territorial superior court has supervisory jurisdiction over tribunals exercising authority within its territory.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and District Judge exercised jurisdiction under the rent law within the territories covered by the Court of the Judicial Commissioner.
The appeal challenged that court’s authority to supervise those bodies.
issues.conclusion: The Rent Controller and District Judge were tribunals within the meaning of Article 227, and Article 227(1), read with Article 241, conferred supervisory jurisdiction over them because they exercised authority within the court’s territory.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227(1), read with Article 241, confers supervisory power over courts and tribunals functioning within the relevant territory. The words “in relation to which” qualify “territories,” not “courts and tribunals.”

predicates.supervision_scope_dispute: The proceeding disputed whether a territorial superior court could supervise a tribunal.
predicates.local_tribunal_exercised_authority: A tribunal exercised adjudicative authority within the territory in question.
predicates.supervisory_court_covers_territory: The superior court’s jurisdiction extended throughout the territory where the tribunal exercised authority.

issues.definition: When a proceeding disputes territorial supervisory authority, a tribunal exercising adjudicative authority within the territory of a superior court falls within that court’s supervisory reach.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional superintendence includes judicial supervision, but must be exercised sparingly to keep subordinate bodies within their authority rather than to correct mere errors.
material_facts: The court considered whether the constitutional power of superintendence was only administrative.
The constitutional text stated that the specific powers listed did not prejudice the generality of the broader supervisory power.
A restriction on questioning judgments that had appeared in an earlier constitutional enactment was omitted from the current text.

The court relied on the judicial understanding of the earlier supervisory provisions described in Moti Lal v. The State through Shrimati Sagrawati and on Dalmia Jain Airways Ltd. v. Sukumar Mukherjee regarding the proper restraint in exercising supervision.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional power includes judicial superintendence, independently of other revisional powers, but is to be exercised most sparingly and only in appropriate cases to keep subordinate bodies within their authority, not to correct mere errors.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227’s general supervisory power is judicial as well as administrative. Its text preserves the generality of the power, and the omission of the restrictive provision formerly found in section 224(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, supports that construction. Moti Lal v. The State through Shrimati Sagrawati was cited on the restoration of judicial superintendence; Dalmia Jain Airways Ltd. v. Sukumar Mukherjee was cited for the sparing exercise of that power.

predicates.judicial_supervision_scope_dispute: The proceeding disputed whether constitutional superintendence extended to judicial rather than only administrative oversight.
predicates.general_supervision_language_preserved: The constitutional text preserved the generality of the supervisory power despite listing particular supervisory functions.
predicates.restrictive_judgment_limit_omitted: The constitutional text omitted a restriction on questioning judgments that had appeared in an earlier enactment.

issues.definition: Where a dispute concerns the scope of judicial supervision, preservation of general supervisory language together with omission of the earlier judgment restriction means that constitutional superintendence includes judicial control.

issues.legal_issue: Supervisory intervention is appropriate when subordinate bodies arbitrarily decline to make an order required by law after a tenant admits arrears and fails to make the required payment.
material_facts: The tenants admitted that rent was unpaid and had not paid it as required by the rent arrangement or at the first hearing.
The Rent Controller declined to order eviction because the tenants were awaiting fixation of a fair rent.
The District Judge acknowledged that the applicable law required an eviction order upon non-payment but declined to apply that requirement because of the tenants’ asserted misunderstanding.
The Judicial Commissioner set aside the lower decisions and ordered eviction; the Supreme Court found no ground to interfere with that action.
issues.conclusion: The lower bodies acted arbitrarily and refused to exercise jurisdiction vested in them by law, so the case called for supervisory interference. The Judicial Commissioner acted properly, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, as extended to Himachal Pradesh, including its proviso, the tenant was required to make the prescribed payment to avoid eviction. Article 227 permits sparing intervention where a subordinate body refuses to exercise jurisdiction vested in it or acts arbitrarily, rather than merely making an error.

rule.if: supervisory_review_of_subordinate_rent_decisions and applicable_rent_rule_made_ejectment_mandatory and arrears_admitted and required_payment_not_made and lower_bodies_declined_order and lower_bodies_knew_mandatory_position

predicates.supervisory_review_of_subordinate_rent_d: The proceeding sought supervisory review of decisions made by subordinate bodies in a rent dispute.
predicates.applicable_rent_rule_made_ejectment_mand: The applicable rent rule required an eviction order when a tenant failed to make the payment required to avoid eviction.
predicates.arrears_admitted: The tenant admitted that rent was in arrears.
predicates.required_payment_not_made: The tenant did not make the payment required to avoid eviction.
predicates.lower_bodies_declined_order: The subordinate bodies declined to order eviction despite the admitted non-payment.
predicates.lower_bodies_knew_mandatory_position: The subordinate bodies recognized that the applicable law required an eviction order upon non-payment.

issues.definition: When a rent-review proceeding concerns admitted arrears, a required payment is not made, and subordinate bodies knowingly decline an order that the applicable rule requires, supervisory interference is justified.
